name: Pregnant Woman
baseMeaning: A picture of a woman standing with one hand resting on her rounded belly. Read in a message it lands as announcing or celebrating a pregnancy.
tldr: 🤰 Pregnant Woman. In a chat it comes across as announcing or celebrating a pregnancy.

contextMeanings.meaning: The plain reading: a woman standing with one hand resting on her rounded belly. Nothing hidden in the drawing itself.
contextMeanings.example: A first pregnancy announcement to family 🤰

contextMeanings.meaning: Borrowed as a reaction, it reads as announcing or celebrating a pregnancy.
contextMeanings.example: Congratulating a friend who just shared news 🤰

contextMeanings.meaning: In a dating thread the gesture is usually doing the work of a line that was not typed. It arrives as announcing or celebrating a pregnancy, softened by whatever sentence sits next to it.

In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — announcing or celebrating a pregnancy — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.

platformNotes.note: In Slack 🤰 lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for a first pregnancy announcement to family, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.
On Discord 🤰 is a staple of the reaction bar, which is why it so often arrives stripped of its announcing or celebrating a pregnancy reading — a shape pressed rather than a message sent.

On X and Twitter 🤰 does most of its work in replies, where it tags a message like congratulating a friend who just shared news. Short enough to survive being the whole post, which is exactly why it is used that way.

On iOS the Pregnant Woman 🤰 renders as the neutral drawing, and the neutral swatch is what most people send without thinking about it. A message like a first pregnancy announcement to family is the kind that carries it — the picture lands before the sentence does.

WhatsApp renders 🤰 exactly as the phone system does, but the keyboard keeps it in the family section, where nobody looks unless they are hunting for it. In family threads it tends to accompany a message like congratulating a friend who just shared news.

generationalNotes.note: Gen Z reaches for 🤰 to do the work of a first pregnancy announcement to family, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is announcing or celebrating a pregnancy.

Millennials tend to send 🤰 deliberately, usually for something like congratulating a friend who just shared news, and they read announcing or celebrating a pregnancy into it more often than the older cohorts do.
Gen X mostly uses 🤰 literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read announcing or celebrating a pregnancy into it than younger senders are.
Older senders use 🤰 in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the announcing or celebrating a pregnancy subtext in it.

warnings.title: 🤰 and 👶 get swapped
warnings.description: The Baby 👶 is one tap away in every picker, and it does not carry the same reading — the baby is the new arrival, the pregnancy is the wait, and the two get swapped in timelines. Check which one you actually picked.

warnings.title: The reading it usually gets is not the one it was sent with

seoTitle: 🤰 Pregnant Woman Emoji - What It Actually Means in Text
seoDescription: 🤰 Pregnant Woman meaning: announcing or celebrating a pregnancy. How the emoji is used at work, at home and in dating threads, and where it goes wrong.

longForm.overview:
The drawing of 🤰 is a woman standing with one hand resting on her rounded belly. It arrived with Unicode 13.0 in the family section, and in a conversation it does the work of a line somebody left out on purpose.

The line it stands in for is announcing or celebrating a pregnancy. That is the reading most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one — a picture carries the same meaning as the sentence it replaces, and it arrives first.

The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets used as a generic celebration picture though it is really a pregnancy announcement, so sending it as filler for a new job or a graduation lands wrong. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is 👶 Baby: the baby is the new arrival, the pregnancy is the wait, and the two get swapped in timelines. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.

The pregnant woman also exists in five skin tones. They are separate pages with separate copy, because picking a tone is a decision in a way that picking the plain emoji is not: it says something about who the sender thinks the reader is.

In short — the pregnant woman reads as announcing or celebrating a pregnancy, it is most often used for a first pregnancy announcement to family or congratulating a friend who just shared news, and the five tone pages under it each say something different about who is sending it. The rest of the page takes those three apart.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
Context, not the picture, decides how this lands. 🤰 in a work thread is congratulating a friend who just shared news; 🤰 in a family thread is a first pregnancy announcement to family; 🤰 in a thread with somebody you like is a way of saying something you would rather not type out.

The tone versions of the emoji make the same point from the other side. The gesture is identical in all five, and the swatch says something about the sender before a word is read.

The shortest messages are the risky ones. A lone 🤰 is the whole reply, and it is carrying a meaning nobody wrote down — announcing or celebrating a pregnancy is the intention, but what arrives is a drawing. Everything the sentence would have disambiguated is simply missing.

Put it this way. A first pregnancy announcement to family is the job the pregnant woman does most: it saves a sentence and lands faster than one would have. Congratulating a friend who just shared news is the job it does second: there the picture is not the point, it is the temperature of the message.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Think about what the emoji is replacing. If the sentence under it is doing the real work, 🤰 will get used as a generic celebration picture though it is really a pregnancy announcement, so sending it as filler for a new job or a graduation lands wrong instead, and the thread ends up carrying a meaning nobody wrote.

And keep it away from first contact. There is nothing warm in the drawing, and a pregnant woman gesture used to answer other people's messages tends to sound like it is settling a point.

Keep it out of the formal register. In a thread about somebody's work, or in a message to somebody you have not met, 🤰 reads as announcing or celebrating a pregnancy, and formality is exactly where that reading does the most damage.

Leave 👶 Baby for the other message. The baby is the new arrival, the pregnancy is the wait, and the two get swapped in timelines. And keep 🤰 out of threads where somebody is hurting: it reads as announcing or celebrating a pregnancy there, because there is nothing in the drawing that says you meant well.
longForm.howToReply:
The safe move in an unclear thread is to answer the text. 🤰 gets used as a generic celebration picture though it is really a pregnancy announcement, so sending it as filler for a new job or a graduation lands wrong often enough that the sentence matters more than the picture.

And do not send 🤰 alone when the message underneath is supposed to be warm. A message like a first pregnancy announcement to family carries the feeling; the picture on its own leaves the reader choosing between announcing or celebrating a pregnancy and something sharper.

Start by reading what the 🤰 was doing. If it was a reaction, react: 🤰 back, and the thread is closed. If it was aimed at you, write. The difference matters, because the reply to a reaction can be a picture and the reply to a request cannot.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🤰 and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under pregnant woman show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.

faqs.question: What does 🤰 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 🤰 is used for announcing or celebrating a pregnancy. The drawing shows a woman standing with one hand resting on her rounded belly, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 🤰 and 👶?
faqs.answer: The baby is the new arrival, the pregnancy is the wait, and the two get swapped in timelines. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

faqs.question: Is 🤰 rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as announcing or celebrating a pregnancy, but it gets used as a generic celebration picture though it is really a pregnancy announcement, so sending it as filler for a new job or a graduation lands wrong. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

faqs.question: What does 🤰 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

conversationExamples.interpretation: A public sign-off, with the emoji as the full stop. The picture is doing the punctuation, which is why it is sent instead of a sentence.

conversationExamples.message: a first pregnancy announcement to family 🤰
conversationExamples.interpretation: The everyday use: the picture carries the whole line. It lands as announcing or celebrating a pregnancy, and matching it with the same emoji is a normal reply.

conversationExamples.message: congratulating a friend who just shared news 🤰
conversationExamples.interpretation: A handover or a sign-off in a channel. It reads as announcing or celebrating a pregnancy, and naming the next step in words is usually clearer than leaving it to the gesture.

conversationExamples.message: there is something you should know 🤰
conversationExamples.interpretation: A small joke or a nudge, with the emoji doing the tone work. It gets used as a generic celebration picture though it is really a pregnancy announcement, so sending it as filler for a new job or a graduation lands wrong more easily here than it does in a work thread, because the thread is thinner.

conversationExamples.message: a first pregnancy announcement to family 🤰
conversationExamples.interpretation: Family threads are where this lands most naturally. The reading is announcing or celebrating a pregnancy, and nobody in the thread is reading it as anything sharper than that.
